rows.title: Sharpness
rows.text: If you are a domestic cat, you see about a third of the fine detail a human sees, 10 cycles a degree against a human's 30. If you are a cheetah, you see about 25 cycles a degree, close to what a human sees. Nobody has measured how sharply the other cats see.
rows.note: Left out the Lynx lynx estimate (R4, grade i) and the qualitative Panthera note (R3), since sharpness only travels within a genus.

rows.title: Color
rows.text: If you are a domestic cat, you have two kinds of color-sensing cell, one most sensitive to blue light and one most sensitive to green. The cheetah, the bobcat and the leopard have the blue-sensing cells too. Nobody has measured how many kinds of color-sensing cell the other cats have, or which colors theirs favor.

cites.taxon: Acinonyx jubatus, Lynx rufus, Panthera pardus

rows.note: R3 is a dog measurement, so I left it out; no record gives peak sensitivities for any wild cat.

rows.title: Pupil
rows.text: If you are a domestic cat, serval, ocelot or fishing cat, your pupil is a vertical slit. If you are a lion, tiger, leopard, jaguar, mountain lion or cheetah, your pupil is round. If you are a bobcat, caracal, Canada lynx or Iberian lynx, your pupil is close to round.
rows.note: Left out the Eurasian lynx (oval to rhomboid, R4) and the species with only carried or unknown grades to keep the row short.

rows.title: Field of view
rows.text: If you are a domestic cat, each of your eyes sees from 90 degrees out on its own side to 30 degrees past straight ahead. Other cats of your genus, Felis, such as the African wildcat and the sand cat, you very likely share this with. Nobody has measured how wide the field is in lions, bobcats, cheetahs or the other cats outside that genus.
rows.note: Left out the 140 degree binocular figure (R2) because it conflicts with R1, whose limits allow about 60 degrees of overlap. Removed the derived 120 degree figure.

rows.title: Dim light
rows.text: If you are a domestic cat, the reflective layer at the back of your eye, the tapetum, reflects up to 130 times more light than the back of a human eye, and you can detect light up to 7 times fainter than a human can. If you are a lion, you have a tapetum too, and it is large and milky blue. Nobody has measured how faint a light a lion or most other cats can detect.
rows.note: Tapetum is unrecorded for bobcat, cheetah, ocelot and most others; leopard, jaguar and tiger only carried from lion, so they are not named.

rows.title: Depth
rows.text: A mouse 20 centimeters from your nose is probably a blur. If you are a domestic cat, you probably cannot focus on anything closer than about 25 centimeters, and your two eyes see the same scene across about 140 degrees, about as much overlap as a human has. Nobody has measured either one in lions, lynx, bobcats or most other cats.
rows.note: Left out R3 (slit-pupil blur): it is modeled for vertical slit pupils, and pupil shape travels only within a genus, so it does not cover lions, tigers or other round-pupil cats.

rows.title: Sharpest spot
rows.text: If you are a domestic cat, your color-sensing cells of the middle kind are packed densest in one spot toward the temple side of the back of each eye. If you are a cheetah, those cells form a horizontal streak instead, and if you are a Spanish wildcat, the cones in your spot are more than twice as dense as a domestic cat's. Nobody has measured where the sharpest spot lies in any other cat.
rows.note: Left out R4 (Panthera tapetum remark, genus-level and not a measured location for other cats).
